name: Pizzicato-Stone
geological_features: Surface covered in billions of small, uniform spherical concretions
Shallow impact craters with concretion-filled floors
Exposed mineral veins cutting through the concretion layer
specific_features: The Plucked Surface — a terrain of loose stone spheres that bounce and scatter at the slightest disturbance
Mineral geodes among the concretions containing crystallized interiors
resources: Iron oxide concretions with industrial applications
Manganese nodules mixed with the surface concretions
description: Pizzicato-Stone is a tiny rocky body whose entire surface is carpeted in billions of small, perfectly spherical stone concretions ranging from marble to basketball size. Walking on the surface in the micro-gravity is like walking on ball bearings — every step sends concretions bouncing away in lazy arcs, clicking and rattling against each other in a cascade that can travel for kilometers.

The airless surface means there is no sound in the conventional sense, but the vibrations transmitted through boot contact create a tactile percussion that EVA crews describe as feeling like plucked strings. The visual effect of a disturbed concretion field is mesmerizing — thousands of stone spheres arcing through space in slow motion, catching the light as they tumble.

The concretions formed in an ancient aqueous environment, when the body was embedded within a larger, water-bearing planetoid that has since broken apart. Each sphere is a geological time capsule, preserving the chemistry of the ancient water in its layered interior. Some contain crystallized geode cores of surprising beauty, and a brisk trade in Pizzicato geodes has developed among collectors.

The body's negligible gravity makes it easy to access but difficult to work on — any surface activity sends concretions flying, and the accumulation of disturbed material in orbit around the body has become a navigation hazard. A cleanup operation using magnetic sweepers has been proposed but not yet funded, and in the meantime, approach vectors to Pizzicato-Stone must account for a growing cloud of orbiting stone spheres.
